name: Chloe Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for speaking with me, Chloe. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I came home after medical school, so I'm the junior doctor at Valley Health Clinic in the farming town where I grew up. It's busy: farm injuries, sheep-dip rashes, pregnant women who live forty minutes out, and older folk who'd rather talk about the weather than their blood pressure. I see about twenty patients a day and do one afternoon of home visits on the hill farms.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know half the waiting room from church or school. What wears me out is not having a specialist down the corridor, so I'm on the phone to the hospital an hour away when I'm not sure, and I'm often not sure yet. We started using a dictation tool this year once the other two doctors had tried it, and I use it most days now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a lot of people round here would be quietly pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we knew it all along, the real work is still people. At church on Sunday I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. This town is short of doctors, so my job is safe, and I rent a little cottage for not much. I've got about three months saved, and I'm careful with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the dictation tool, because it gets me home earlier. I'd keep studying for my exams and saving a bit each month towards buying a share in the clinic one day. And I'd keep helping my dad at his hardware shop on Saturday mornings when he's short-handed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your dad's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Online sellers have been eating into it for years, and that won't change. But my dad's stubborn. Farmers still want someone to tell them which bolt to buy, and that's why my dad's hardware shop is still open. If it ever got bad, I'd help him, and my brother would too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything at work worrying you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only my own learning. I'm still not quick with the complicated older patients, and I want the senior doctor, Dr Owens, to trust me with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds sensible. Not too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should take the tools that clearly help and leave the rest. I'd say the clinic, not some office in the capital, should decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a town like ours would actually benefit, because we can't get enough doctors. If AI handles the letters and bookings, I'd have more time for home visits. The worry is the health board deciding small clinics only need one doctor and a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until Dr Owens and the other doctor had tried each new tool, then use what works, same as the dictation. I'd make myself the one who does the hands-on things, like stitching and the hill farm visits. And I'd keep saving, maybe a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, mostly about decisions being made far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would make those decisions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The health board, mostly people who've never driven our roads in winter. The health board looks at a spreadsheet and sees three doctors. The board doesn't see the old man who won't come in until his leg's black.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm fine and the town still needs me. That's what they'd want to hear, and I think it's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Goodness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should slow it down in medicine until we know it's safe. I'd say it at church and to anyone at the clinic, gently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried for myself. Most of what I do is thinking: deciding, prescribing, phoning the hospital. That goes in 2028, and the hands-on work, stitches and examinations, goes when robots come around 2031. Out here robots might take longer to arrive, but I can't count on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dr Owens to let me take on all the procedures and home visits. I'd stop saving for the clinic share and keep the money as a cushion instead. And I'd talk to my dad about working more hours at the shop if the clinic cut me back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying about it a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving medicine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. I'd hold on while there's still something useful for me to do. If it came to it, I could run the shop with my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the town lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A face they know. People here will tell me things in the kitchen they'd never type into a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. A bit more time to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a chance to plan for towns like ours, not just cities. I'd write to our local representative about keeping a doctor in every small town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be qualified by then and settled. But the deciding part of my job would go in 2031, and the hands-on part around 2034. I'd still be young, which is good, but it's my whole career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pass my exams and then train in minor surgery and emergency care, because out here there's nobody else when a farmer gets hurt. I'd use the AI tools once they're proven, so I'm not left behind. And I'd keep saving rather than buying into the clinic yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than with two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you marry or start a family in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to, if the right person comes along. I wouldn't let a computer decide that for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People in cities designing things for cities. Nobody asked a hill farmer what a hill farm needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to do this properly, so let's do it with care. I'd talk about it at the clinic's planning meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel a lot better. I'd be an experienced rural doctor, maybe a partner, and hands-on work would last until around 2039. The town would still need someone it trusts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy into the clinic in a few years, as I always planned. I'd train in emergency care and pick up AI tools as they become normal. And I'd keep helping my dad at the shop, because family comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a student from your town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a student from our town to come home after training, because small places will need people they trust more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that still worries you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the health board uses the ten years to plan us away. I'd keep an eye on that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd barely be qualified. What would help is a rule that every small town keeps a real doctor, and decisions made by people who know the place.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what keeps me going. It's the people and my faith. If the whole job changed, I'd still want to be the one who drives up the hill when someone's in trouble.
